cells.tense: The heart is open right now, before there is anything in particular to feel about.
cells.act: let yourself be drawn before you choose
cells.ask: Follow a pull partway before you settle what it means — ten minutes, no conclusion. Stay with it while it stays unnamed, then set it down without acting.
cells.core:
You can stand in an opening. Something in you is ready to feel before there's a name for what's coming, and the not-knowing doesn't scare you — you let it stay undecided and remain alongside it.

What that's good for: in a place where something false just came down, the first honest feeling surfaces before any sense is made of it, and you're available for that. The pull comes before you settle anything — that's the order. So when something draws you, follow it partway, past the first reflex to label what it means. Notice the pull, name what it wants, and stop there for now. Feelings gather into a shape you didn't order, and you get the read before you commit to it. That's what this opening is for.
cells.sheetLine: The pull comes before you settle anything, and you can let it.
cells.verb: standing open to what hasn't arrived yet
cells.place: where what was built on a false premise comes down

cells.tense: The whole arrival is being rehearsed in advance, and nothing is allowed to land unfinished.
cells.act: finish the legacy by sustained will
cells.ask: Choose something you're forcing to a close right now, and ease off it for a day. If a step is truly due, take that one from calm, not pressure.
cells.core:
When something opens, you get ahead of it — you picture how it lands, what it means, what it will require, before any of that has happened. The staying open gets turned into a project. You're trying to have it finished and settled and known, and a thing that just began can't be handed to you on those terms.

What's out of step: your will is running ahead of what's actually here, and the pace is costing you the very openness you're trying to protect. So choose something you're forcing to a close and ease off it for a day — not abandoning it, just letting it not be done yet. If a real step is due, take that one from a settled place, and the unfinished parts can stay that way. The form holds when it's finished from calm, not from bracing.
cells.sheetLine: You're completing it before it's had a chance to arrive.
cells.verb: standing open to what hasn't arrived yet
cells.place: where what was built on a false premise comes down

cells.tense: The opening happened once, and you are still at that door, which is already behind you.
cells.act: let what was only possible stand finished
cells.ask: Bring something that already got its start all the way finished — one sitting, no more. Carry it there this week, until it stands without needing you.
cells.core:
Something opened in you once — a feeling, a direction, a charge — and you keep touching the memory of it rather than the live thing. You can describe the day it started better than you can say what it became. The live opening isn't here with you right now. You're at a door you already walked through.

What pulls you back: the beginning is where you feel capable, and starting again is safer than carrying. So bring something that already got its start all the way finished — a completed page, a sent message, a thing that stands without you. One sitting. When it stands finished, what was only a spark becomes something you're beside, and a new moment can reach you from there.
cells.sheetLine: It started. You're still at the door it opened.
cells.verb: standing open to what hasn't arrived yet
cells.place: where what was built on a false premise comes down

cells.tense: An exchange with someone is running in one direction while you keep no account of it.
cells.act: give one thing and take one thing, in balance
cells.ask: With someone, say out loud what you gave and what you need. Then hold off on fixing it — no efficiency required, no clearing it out.
cells.core:
There's an exchange running between you and someone, and you don't count it. You're steady about what you do for people and slightly blind to what you take or need back, and the exchange looks fair to you because you're not the one keeping score. It stays that way by nobody naming it.

The hand doing this is yours. So with someone, say out loud what you gave and what you need, and hold off on fixing it up. You don't have to even it out on the spot. If the other person offers something, take it at the honest size. That puts the balance into daylight where it can be seen and adjusted — which is different from being quietly assumed.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the exchange fair by not looking at it.
cells.verb: standing open to what hasn't arrived yet
cells.place: where what was built on a false premise comes down

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I'm most exposed to is in the Unacknowledged cell: that the person is the quiet one who gives more than they take. The record shows Reciprocity operating with authorship misattributed — it doesn't show which way the imbalance runs, so a reader could fairly say the giving isn't the pattern, or that the weighing is real and not quiet. The asks survive: each one works whether the person is the one who over-gives or simply the one who hasn't put the exchange into plain sight. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you're the one who's always giving.' I've written the cell without it.
